reference.source: Apley & Solomon / standard sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: Presents with posterior heel or lower-calf pain and stiffness that is worst on starting activity and after rest, with local tendon thickening and tenderness
It is divided into mid-portion disease (a few centimetres above the insertion) and insertional disease at the calcaneal attachment, which are managed differently
The mid-portion tendon has a relatively hypovascular zone that predisposes it to degenerative failure under repetitive load
It is a degenerative tendinopathy with disorganised collagen and neovascularisation rather than true tendinitis
Always distinguish tendinopathy from a complete rupture; a positive Thompson (calf squeeze) test and a palpable gap indicate rupture and need urgent referral
Progressive eccentric or heavy slow-resistance calf loading is the cornerstone of treatment for mid-portion disease
Insertional disease may respond less well to full-range eccentric loading and often needs modified, reduced-dorsiflexion exercises and heel lifts
Corticosteroid injection into or around the tendon is generally avoided because of the risk of rupture
Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are associated with tendinopathy and tendon rupture and should be considered in the history
reference.pathophysiology: Achilles tendinopathy is an overuse condition in which repetitive loading exceeds the tendon's capacity to adapt, causing microtears and a failed healing response. Histology shows collagen disorganisation, increased ground substance, and neovascularisation with accompanying nerve ingrowth rather than inflammatory cells. The mid-portion watershed zone of relative hypovascularity is vulnerable, while insertional disease involves the enthesis and may be associated with a Haglund deformity or retrocalcaneal bursitis.
additionalDifferentials: Complete or partial Achilles tendon rupture
Posterior ankle impingement or os trigonum
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound to show tendon thickening, hypoechoic areas, neovascularity, and to detect partial tears
MRI for detailed assessment in refractory or surgical cases and to characterise insertional pathology
Plain radiographs for insertional disease to identify calcification, a Haglund deformity, or spur
Consider metabolic and inflammatory screening in atypical, bilateral, or young patients
redFlags: Sudden pain with a palpable gap and positive Thompson test indicating tendon rupture
Recent fluoroquinolone use raising rupture risk
Night pain, systemic symptoms, or a mass suggesting infection or tumour
Inflammatory or bilateral enthesitis suggesting spondyloarthropathy
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve over three to six months with structured loading, though symptoms can be slow to settle and recurrence is common; insertional disease is generally more resistant to conservative treatment than mid-portion disease.
pitfalls: Missing a tendon rupture by not performing the Thompson test
Injecting corticosteroid into or around the tendon and precipitating rupture
Applying mid-portion eccentric protocols to insertional disease and worsening symptoms
Advancing loading too quickly and provoking flares, or ignoring contributory training errors
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
management: Progressive mechanical loading as the cornerstone: eccentric or heavy slow-resistance calf loading for mid-portion disease, with limited-dorsiflexion loading for insertional disease
Relative rest with load and activity modification and graded return, plus simple analgesia and short-term NSAIDs for pain
Address footwear and contributory factors, including a heel raise for insertional disease and correction of training errors and biomechanical faults
Extracorporeal shockwave therapy as an adjunct for refractory cases
Use injections cautiously, avoiding intratendinous corticosteroid because of rupture risk, and consider high-volume or sclerosing injection in selected cases
Distinguish and urgently refer a suspected complete rupture indicated by a positive Thompson calf-squeeze test and a palpable gap
Surgery such as tendon debridement, or excision of a Haglund deformity in insertional disease, for cases failing prolonged conservative treatment
